California Sea Lion (Zalophus californianus)   Scientific Classification 	•	Kingdom: Animalia 	•	Phylum: Chordata 	•	Class: Mammalia 	•	Order: Carnivora 	•	Family: Otariidae (Eared seals) 	•	Genus: Zalophus 	•	Species: Zalophus californianus  Description Large marine mammals with streamlined, brown to dark brown bodies and external ear flaps. Males are larger with pronounced sagittal crests on their heads, while females are smaller with sleeker profiles. This observation shows a dense group hauled out on a floating dock, a common social resting behavior.  Habitat Observed in a harbor area in Newport, Oregon. California sea lions inhabit coastal waters, beaches, rocky shores, and marinas along the Pacific coast of North America, from British Columbia to Baja California.  Additional Notes 	•	Life stage: Mixed group of adults and juveniles. 	•	Sex: Likely both males and females present. 	•	Behavior: Resting closely together on a dock, likely for warmth, social bonding, and predator avoidance. Occasional vocalizations and flipper movements were noted. 	•	Ecological role: marine predators that help regulate fish populations; also serve as prey for orcas and large sharks.

Reported to the Marine Mammal Center and received this response: "This is an elephant seal pup venturing out on their own for the first time. Since they are still so young, they tend to get tired easily and come up onto the beach to rest. Elephant seal pups are ok to be out of the water and, once they are feeling more rested, they will venture back out to the ocean to eat. The best way to help young elephant seals like this one is to stay at least 50 feet away at all times and keep dogs on leash. We have taken a number of calls for this animal Other than the people and dogs, we are not particularly concerned for this animal. It is a little underweight and alert. We are monitoring the situation and we are hoping that people will give it time and space to rest and that it will return to the ocean when it has had a chance to rest."

Sarasota Christmas Bird Count with Valeri Ponzo, Sue Guarasci, Mary Heinlen, and Carolyn Primus. Only those spots where I took one or more photographs are listed):  0715-0950: John and Mabel Ringling Museum of Art -- By far our best area. But high tide was in the morning, and the banyan hammocks were really quiet of landbirds. Because the museum grounds are also a botanical garden, I was careful to include only non-cultivated species. Also, I was carrying my scope, severely limiting my ability to take cell-phone photographs.  1038-1105: New lake east of Sun Hydraulics -- We found sea ducks here.  1136-1157: New College (northern part) -- The tide was still high, inundating all but one small mudflat. We left quickly.  1224-1255: Charles Hegener Memorial Nature Walk -- A short 20-foot wide walk to Sarasota Bay. The vegetation is a mix of native coastal strand and various exotics that have moved in from the adjacent neighborhood.  1303-1308: Beach Park  1312-1321: Whitaker Greenway Park -- Most of the park was fenced off, resulting in a very quick visit.  1326-1438: Van Wezel Performing Arts Hall/Rampa Lido Key Waterfront Park -- We saw some waterbirds here --including one that was studied closely -- and we ate lunch here.  1538: Retention pond east of Booker T. Washington School.  1609-1613: Pond at the southwest corner of Bradenton Road and Mecca Drive.  1633-1709: Field south of the lake east of Sun Hydraulics/Sun Hydraulics -- The field was recently mowed, so we found only one Savannah Sparrow.  1729-1804: Heron roost at the Sarasota Lakes RV Resort -- we arrived at least 30 minutes too late to see the birds fly in.  We ended the day with 72 species.

West Pasco Christmas Bird Count, solo in the morning and late afternoon, with Don Fraser in the early afternoon.  Our itinerary for today was:  0649-1110: Hudson Beach Park -- The weather at the start was pre-sunrise, 47 degrees ("feels like" 41), and with NE winds at 12 MPH. The tide was outgoing and the strong NE winds pushed exacerbated the low water levels by pushing out much water and many birds out of the bay. It was slow going, but there were enough "good" birds to keep it interesting. My best birds of the morning -- unique to the CBC this day -- were Horned Grebe and American Oystercatcher. I left at 1110 and headed to the countdown lunch.  ????-????: Anclote Gulf Park -- with Don Fraser; I kept no photographs from here. We came searching for Whimbrel on one particular jetty but it was not present, so we left within 20 minutes.  1426-1508: Green Key Park -- with Don Fraser; we did not find any of our afternoon targets.  1536-1755: Hudson Beach Park -- afternoon watch; I was solo again. It was slower than the morning and I almost quit around 1720. At 1723, a single American White Pelican flew by south to north -- my third unique bird for the CBC on this day -- so I stayed until it was nearly dark. The weather at the end was post-sunset, 61 degrees ("feels like" 59), with ENE winds at 10 MPH. It was highish tide.  I left at almost 1758 and headed home.

With Valeri Ponzo (in part); an unsuccessful search for the Yellow-headed Caracara in Miami. This morning at 0729 Val texted me to see if I had plans for the weekend. I did not, so we planned a trip for the caracara, which Val had not yet chased. Val was in Titusville visiting family, so I spent an hour birding on my own before Val arrived home. We left shortly afterward.  Our itinerary for today was:  1130-1230: Payne Park, Sarasota -- A solo visit while Val was still en route home. This was my first visit in several years. I stayed in the northern half of the park and walked west to A.B. Smith Park. The weather at the start was sunny, 60 degrees ("feels like" 58), and breezy.  1517-1530: Collier County Rest Area along Alligator Alley -- a potty stop and a brief iNatting session, but we were pressed for time so did not linger.  1656-1730: Oleta River State Park -- to have better luck at finding the caracara, we split up, with Val at Angelfish/Pufferfish/Panther Pavilion to the north, and me at Pelican Pavilion to the south. I photographed a first-cycle Bonaparte's Gull that was less than 10 feet off the beach. When it saw me, it swam then walked up to me. I expected it to have a fish hook in it, or for it to have been wrapped in fishing line, but it had neither. I went back to looking for the caracara for a minutes or two and the gull had absolutely vanished. The weather was sunny, mild, and breezy.

With Valeri Ponzo; another unsuccessful search for the Yellow-headed Caracara (after missing it yesterday afternoon). We were so exhausted by today's activities that we left after leaving OIeta River State Park; my pedometer app stated that I walked 8.8 miles today, most of it at Haulover Beach Park.  Our itinerary for today was:  0627-1201: Haulover Beach Park -- We parked at the coordinates between the Bill Bird Marina building and the pickleball courts, where the caracara was seen flying into the park yesterday morning. Nothing. So while Val stayed around that spot, I walked down to the bait shop and back three times, scanning the Coconut Palms nearly constantly, then walked north to the northern parking lot once, then once more to the bait shop, where Val picked me up. We explored more of the park, and came to the jetty east of State Road A1A at Haulover Inlet. Neither of us had ever been here before. We were amused that four police cars had intercepted a man with a huge camera lens -- the nude beach is probably within 1000 feet! LOL. Anyway, we enjoyed a flock of Blue-crowned Parakeets here and then spent maybe 30 minutes botanizing weeds in the lawn surrounding the electrical substation. We found a juvenile Brown Pelican that was poorly banded (the band appeared too small and was not crimped tight all around); we got the band combination (1298-24392) and will report it. Then we drove to the northern parking lot (north of the pickleball courts) and spent more time iNatting bugs on the walls of the restrooms and other buildings. I found a shallow puddle in the parking lot that supported three tiny, gray bugs (two of these were copulating); we did what we could photographing them, but they were extremely skittish).The weather at the start was pre-sunrise but cloudy, 73 degrees ("feels like" 73), and with winds from the NE at 14 MPH.  1204-1251: Subway Restaurant just outside Oleta River State Park -- lunch and a chance to sit down and relax. We iNatted the large, weedy planters outside the store after lunch!  1312-1725: Oleta River State Park -- we checked out pavilion areas (Angelfish/Pufferfish/Panther to the north and Pelican to the south) in case the Yellow-headed Caracara was extremely early. A park ranger stopped us and asked if we birders (instead of the typical bird-watchers), because he hasn't seen any birders in the park in a good while. He offered advice on finding the caracara, and then remarked that he had seen the San Blas Jay recently, usually around Panther Pavilion. This is a banded, escaped/released bird that was first found in late fall 2024. I wasn't aware that the jay was still around because eBird no longer sends out rare bird emails for most exotic birds (this is why I divorced eBird in 2022). We botanized the trail between and among the pavilions until about 1630, finding several caterpillars and moths. Then I walked to Pelican Pavilion while Val stayed to the north. Val kept hearing a strange call that she thought was a parakeet or tern until she went to xenocanto.com and realized that she was hearing the San Blas Jay! Val texted me and I ran to Panther Pavilion. The jay was with a Blue Jay (hmmm, interesting) and both were difficult to see as they fed mostly quietly in the canopy of Seagrapes and trees. The light was horrible, looking up at the undersides of two birds against an overcast sky. Val managed two photographs that showed part of the San Blas Jay's blue shoulders. My photographs show only a black bird with pale eyes and a funky-looking long tail -- for an hour or more, I truly thought that I had photographed a Common Grackle! The San Blas Jay called once every 5-10 minutes, and the call did sound like a parakeet or a tern -- a syrupy series of whistles that lasted about one second. It was unlike the harsh notes uttered by many corvids. Eventually, we lost the jays and resumed looking for the caracara. A park employee nicely informed us that the park closes at 1730, so we left a few minutes early. There were surprisingly few families grilling in the park, despite it being Thanksgiving weekend -- the park ranger we spoke with indicated that the caracara shows up in the park more often on days when many people are grilling and producing food to scavenge. The weather at the start was cloudy, 75 degrees ("feels like" 75), and with winds from the NE at 17 MPH. The sun appeared in mid-afternoon for about five minutes, which is when I saw the Mangrove Skipper nectaring. Otherwise, it was cloudy and windy all day; it even sprinkled shortly after we arrived at the park.  We headed west and north immediately, with Val arriving home at 2132, and me arriving home at 2342.  The San Blas Jay was an obvious lifer for each of us, and is my sixth life bird in Florida this year (after photographing Inca Dove, Broad-tailed Hummingbird, Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher, Sage Thrasher, and American Tree Sparrow earlier this year). Val photographed these six plus Gray Gull.

Observed a male White-tailed Deer displaying severe neurologic impairment. The deer was moving in a very even, consistent serpentine pattern on and off the highway. The loops were all roughly the same size, and it stayed locked into that pattern even when interrupted.  It walked directly into my car when I pulled over and blocked its path to the highway, then resumed its serpentine. Several other vehicles narrowly missed it as it would walk right in front of them. The only thing I ever saw somewhat interrupt its path was either a physical barrier or being moved aside.  When I used my car to gently nudge it off the roadway, it immediately began trying to walk straight through a barbed-wire fence without responding to being cut or changing direction. This continued for more than ten minutes.  The deer did not react to moving cars, people, or dogs barking at a close distance. No visible blood or traumatic injuries. No limping. One antler missing. Some missing hair and a noticeable puckering along the back. Body condition not emaciated. Heavy foaming at the mouth. Eyes appeared gooped or swollen shut. Breathing was quick and shallow, but not panting. Behavior was non-aggressive and essentially unresponsive.  Property owners reported it had been weaving in that same small area along the highway for at least two hours before I passed by.  Game warden was unavailable to come out. I reported the case, as did other people, but don't know what came of it.   Posting here to document the case and to hear any informed opinions on possible causes.

Yes, this House Finch landed on my head as I sat on the porch.     I had been sitting watching it for a little while though. It was eating seeds that I had spread on the floor of the porch, and occasionally taking wing - sort of. It flapped its wings furiously, but didn't fly very well. It hovered  in place more than flew forward through the air, and then had trouble gaining oe even maintaining altitude. It would slowly approach a landing spot much like a helicopter slows down and gently approaches a chosen spot. It seemed to only be able to reach about 6 to 8 feet off the ground, and then would start a drifting slow descending approach to its next landing spot. I very much thought this was a fledgling on its first minutes out of a nest, but I did not see any parent birds attending its efforts or attempting to guide or feed it. It frequently voiced a simple chirp, and apparently was not at all afraid of my watching it at close quarters.     I was quite startled that it made my hat covered head the object of one of its slow landing approaches. It stayed there for as long as it took me to slowly fish my phone out of my trouser pocket, switch cameras from front to back, and awkwardly make its picture. I am not one that ever "takes selfies," so I am surprised when the time came I managed this as well as I did. The exposure was not great, as the lighting was pretty unbalanced between the foreground and background, but I've adjusted that a bit in "postproduction."     Was it indeed an inexperienced fledgling, rather than an injured or mentally deranged bird? Regardless, I watched it on and off all day long. Toward evening it seemed to have a bit more control in flight, and was able to land repeatedly on a small window mounted seed feeder. I put a dish of water on the floor for it, and the next day, it seemed to spend a good amount of time on the feeder. The following day, I could not tell if it was still among the many House Finches that live here now. None were behaving unusually. I would like to think it gained strength and skill to behave more like a mature flyer, and so become less conspicuous.     In *any* case, I thank this charming bird wherever it is now - fledgling, failure, or whatever it was that day - for making me feel for a little while like Saint Francis, or Snow White.   : )

Southern Sea Otter grooming it’s fur. Sea otters groom themselves meticulously to maintain the insulating quality of their dense fur, which is essential for survival in cold waters.    My favorite close-up Southern Sea Otter (Enhydra lutris ssp. nereis) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=526556&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any  Female with Scarred Nose: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/165516431  Male showing Teeth: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/164818190  Praying: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/175683723  Typical Tail Position: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/151550648    Southern Sea Otter (Enhydra lutris ssp. nereis) is a Pacific Ocean marine dwelling mammal in the Mustelids (Mustelidae) family that grows 3.5-4.5 ft (up to 1.5 meters) long. Northern Sea Otters are a lot larger than Southern Sea Otters, so they are probably the largest weasel. Unlike most marine mammals, the sea otter's primary form of insulation is an exceptionally thick coat of fur, the densest in the animal kingdom. Although it can walk on land, the sea otter is capable of living exclusively in the ocean. Sea Otters are usually seen resting while wrapped up in floating Kelp beds, floating on their backs cracking open seafood with small rocks, eating, sleeping, preening thick fur, carrying one pup, or teaching the pups to dive and find food. Sea Otters eat a variety of shellfish, sea urchins, and especially red fat innkeeper worms in Elkhorn Slough. They do not go after fish. The range of Southern Sea Otters is usually south of San Francisco CA and north of the Channel Islands in southern California.  Conservation Status: Vulnerable and threatened (T) in United States (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service). The numbers of sea otters are holding steady, but the gene pool is very small because their numbers were radically reduced during the fur trade for ladies fashion :-(    California Department of Fish and Wildlife: http://sibr.com/mammals/M164.html  "Sea otters are found in nearshore marine environments of California from Ano Nuevo, San Mateo Co. to Point Sal, Santa Barbara Co. Canopies of giant kelp and bull kelp provide important rafting and feeding areas. Sea otters also forage regularly on clams and crabs in areas of sandy bottom habitat. Population densities in these sandy areas are lower than in more productive rocky-bottom habitats.  Feeding: Feed almost exclusively on marine invertebrates. They are opportunistic foragers, and eat mostly abalones and sea urchins, crabs, and clams in California. Other food items in California include snails, mussels, scallops, chitons, barnacles, squids, octopuses, and starfishes.  Cover: Frequent nearshore waters adjacent to rocky coasts, near points of land, or large bays where kelp beds occur. Often seen sleeping and diving for food in, or near, kelp beds. Often pull one, or more, strands of kelp over body to remain stationary before resting and sleeping. Also raft in open waters off sandy beaches to feed.  Reproduction: No births have been witnessed, but observations suggest births occur on intertidal reefs, and in water.  Water: Good quality, nearshore marine water, free of oil contaminants, is required to protect the insulation property of the fur.  Pattern: Optimal habitats include rocky substrates with ample interstices, where invertebrates can live out of reach of the sea otters. These areas provide a continuing source of food, as individuals move out and become available. Kelp beds also provide cover from high surf and predators.  Activity Patterns: Active yearlong in circadian pattern. Active day or night, with peak feeding in early morning and late afternoon.  Seasonal Movements / Migration: Non-migratory. Males at range peripheries move seasonally in relation to peaks in breeding activity. Females make fewer movements than males.  Territory: Mostly expressed weakly. However, in California, some males leave rafts of males and establish territories adjacent to, or including, rafting areas of females. No other males are allowed to rest in these territories. Females are allowed into these territories, subject to attempts at copulation. These male territories are congruent with home ranges, and smaller than those of nonterritorial males."    "Genetic Link Found Between Deadly Pathogen and Wild and Feral Cats on Land" https://www.ucdavis.edu/news/whats-killing-sea-otters-scientists-pinpoint-parasite-strain  "A current threat to the Southern Sea Otter is an infectious pathogen (Toxoplasma gondii) that spreads from CAT FECES on land to the sea, leading to detrimental impacts on marine wildlife. Rivers and storm drains wash the feline fecal pathogen into the ocean. Wild and domestic cats are the only known hosts of Toxoplasma, in which the parasite forms egglike stages, called oocysts, in their feces. The range of Southern Sea Otters is usually south of San Francisco CA and north of the Channel Islands in southern California.  Conservation Status: Vulnerable and threatened (T) in United States (U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service). The numbers of sea otters are holding steady, but the gene pool is very small because their numbers were radically reduced during the fur trade for ladies fashion :-(      California Department of Fish and Wildlife: http://sibr.com/mammals/M164.html  "Sea otters are found in nearshore marine environments of California from Ano Nuevo, San Mateo Co. to Point Sal, Santa Barbara Co. Canopies of giant kelp and bull kelp provide important rafting and feeding areas. Sea otters also forage regularly on clams and crabs in areas of sandy bottom habitat. Population densities in these sandy areas are lower than in more productive rocky-bottom habitats.  Feeding: Feed almost exclusively on marine invertebrates. They are opportunistic foragers, and eat mostly abalones and sea urchins, crabs, and clams in California. Other food items in California include snails, mussels, scallops, chitons, barnacles, squids, octopuses, and starfishes.  Cover: Frequent nearshore waters adjacent to rocky coasts, near points of land, or large bays where kelp beds occur. Often seen sleeping and diving for food in, or near, kelp beds. Often pull one, or more, strands of kelp over body to remain stationary before resting and sleeping. Also raft in open waters off sandy beaches to feed.  Reproduction: No births have been witnessed, but observations suggest births occur on intertidal reefs, and in water.  Water: Good quality, nearshore marine water, free of oil contaminants, is required to protect the insulation property of the fur.  Pattern: Optimal habitats include rocky substrates with ample interstices, where invertebrates can live out of reach of the sea otters. These areas provide a continuing source of food, as individuals move out and become available. Kelp beds also provide cover from high surf and predators.  Activity Patterns: Active yearlong in circadian pattern. Active day or night, with peak feeding in early morning and late afternoon.  Seasonal Movements / Migration: Non-migratory. Males at range peripheries move seasonally in relation to peaks in breeding activity. Females make fewer movements than males.  Territory: Mostly expressed weakly. However, in California, some males leave rafts of males and establish territories adjacent to, or including, rafting areas of females. No other males are allowed to rest in these territories. Females are allowed into these territories, subject to attempts at copulation. These male territories are congruent with home ranges, and smaller than those of nonterritorial males." Rivers and storm drains wash the feline fecal pathogen into the ocean. Wild and domestic cats are the only known hosts of Toxoplasma, in which the parasite forms egglike stages, called oocysts, in their feces.
